newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Strong demand forecast for UK gilt auctio.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Strong demand forecast for UK gilt auctio.

text.p: Good demand from pension funds and investors looking to cover short positions should ensure Wednesday's auction of British gilts goes smoothly despite concerns that the price is a touch too high, analysts said.
The Bank of England is due to auction 2.5 billion stg of 8.0 percent gilts due 2021 and analysts say the result will be the key domestic influence on Britain's debt market this week.
"Given the demand I'd expect it to be more than twice covered," said Steve Scott, gilts analyst at Kleinwort Benson Securities.
"There are a people out there sitting on short positions and looking to get it back at the auction."
Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW, also thought investors covering short positions would snap up stock at the auction. "Investors are generally a bit short of the market," he said.

Analysts said the auction would appeal to investors looking to raise their exposure to longer maturities and increase the duration of their portfolios. Good demand was likely from institutions, they said.
"The 8.00 percent 2021 stock will appeal particularly to institutional investors such as pension funds," analysts at Merrill Lynch said.
But although analysts said there was strong potential demand, some warned that a light cheapening of the stock was needed ahead of the auction to ensure there was no upset.
"I think it will go off OK, although we might need to see a concession in market levels before we get to it. A bit of steepening would help," Adams said.
"The spread of 20 basis points between 10 and 20 year gilts doesn't look high enough, especially with the recent performance and current levels of the market," he said.
David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy, said a slight widening of the spread with Bunds would be ideal.
"The auction should go reasonably well," he said. "Ironically, the worse gilts perform early this week, the better the auction should go."

If the gilt-Bund spread widened, bargain hunters could be attracted, he said. "172 (basis points) is not great value, more fair value. If that edges out towards 180, the auction will look a better bet," Coleman said.
But Scott at Kleinwort said he thought the current price was low enough. "I think the 2021s have already cheapened enough. We've steepened two or three basis points since the auction was announced."
With no major data due this week, there was little chance of a major price rise forcing investors with short positions to buy before the auction, Scott said.

Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan is due to give his Humphrey Hawkins testimony on the state on the U.S. economy on Wednesday and Thursday, and some analysts say he may try once again to inject a note of caution into world markets.
But Scott said the auction was unlikely to be hit by caution ahead of Greenspan's speech. "If most of the buying is to fill in shorts, it won't be affected," he said.
By 1323 GMT on Monday, the 2021 gilts were quoted at 106.94 to yield 7.375 percent.
